plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to take a claim like 'you should always keep your promises', ask the 4 questions philosophers ask of it (what does it mean, how would we know, is it right, who gets to decide), name one thinker who tackled each question and say in a sentence what they argued.
plan.horizon14: Later, around day 14, you could read one short original text, such as Plato's Apology, and follow the argument without a guide.
plan.horizon28: Later, around day 28, you could explain how one modern debate, such as free speech or AI rights, repeats an argument from 2,000 years ago.

picture.name: A long argument
picture.line: Western philosophy is one dinner-table argument that has run for about 2,500 years, where each new guest answers the one who spoke before, so you only need to know who is replying to whom.

chapters.title: What counts as a good argument
chapters.covers: A claim, the reasons behind it, and how to spot when the reasons do not actually support the claim, using 3 everyday examples.
chapters.outcome: You can take any opinion, split it into its claim and its reasons, and say whether the reasons hold it up.

chapters.title: Socrates and the habit of asking why
chapters.covers: How Socrates questioned people in Athens around 400 BC, why it got him executed, and how to run his question-and-answer method on your own beliefs.
chapters.outcome: You can ask 5 'why' questions in a row about a belief you hold and notice where your answers run out.

chapters.title: Plato and Aristotle: is the real world the one we see?
chapters.covers: Plato's cave story and his idea that perfect forms sit behind everyday things, then Aristotle's reply that we learn by looking closely at the world itself.
chapters.outcome: You can explain the cave story in 3 sentences and say which side, Plato or Aristotle, a scientist is closer to.

chapters.title: Descartes and the question of what we can know
chapters.covers: Descartes doubting everything in 1641 until he hit one thing he could not doubt, and why that moved the argument from the world to the mind.
chapters.outcome: You can explain 'I think, therefore I am' and say what problem it was trying to solve.

chapters.title: Hume and Kant: where knowledge comes from
chapters.covers: Hume's claim that everything we know comes through the senses and habit, and Kant's reply that the mind brings its own rules to experience.
chapters.outcome: You can explain, with the example of cause and effect, why Hume said we never actually see one thing cause another and how Kant answered.

chapters.title: How should I act: Mill against Kant
chapters.covers: Two rival tests for right and wrong: Mill's 'does it produce the most happiness' and Kant's 'could everyone act this way', applied to the same 3 dilemmas.
chapters.outcome: You can run one moral dilemma through both tests and say where they give different answers.

chapters.title: Nietzsche and the modern turn: who decides what is true or good
chapters.covers: Nietzsche's challenge in the 1880s that our values have a history and were made by people, and how that question still shapes today's arguments about truth and power.
chapters.outcome: You can hear a modern claim such as 'that is just your opinion' and place it in the long argument, naming which earlier thinker it echoes and who would push back.
